<SYSTEM>This is the full developer documentation for Optionary</SYSTEM>

# Optionary

> Source-generated options binding and JSON Schema for .NET configuration.

Optionary turns an **options type** into two things, generated from the same model at build time:

* a **binder** that creates the type from its **section** of `IConfiguration` and registers it as `IOptions<T>`, with no reflection, so it is trimming and Native AOT safe;
* a **JSON Schema** for the section. Every assembly carries a **fragment** per section, and each **host** (an application or a test project) **merges** the fragments it can see into one **application schema**, which editors use for completion, hover documentation and validation of `appsettings.json`, YAML and TOML files.

```csharp
using Optionary;


/// <summary>Options for the greetings this library prints.</summary>
[Optionary] // section "Greetings"
public sealed class GreetingsOptions
{
    /// <summary>The text that comes before the name.</summary>
    public string Message { get; set; } = "Hello";
}
```

| Package                        | What it is                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Optionary`                    | The `[Optionary]` attribute, the source generator, the runtime registration and the schema build. |
| `Optionary.Configuration.Yaml` | A YAML configuration provider. It doesn’t depend on `Optionary`.                                  |

## Where to go next

[Section titled “Where to go next”](#where-to-go-next)

* [Getting started](getting-started/): add the package, declare a section, register it and point an editor at the schema.
* [Declarations](guides/declarations/): the class and assembly forms, and how the section path is derived.
* [Key styles](guides/key-styles/): spelling keys in Pascal, camel, dash or underscore case.
* [Binding and validation](guides/binding/): what the generated binder does, and where it deliberately differs from Microsoft’s configuration binding generator.
* [Schema and editors](guides/schema-and-editors/): the library and application schemas, Visual Studio, VS Code and Rider.
* [Registering from a library](guides/registering-from-a-library/): the generated registration method and its contract.
* [YAML provider](guides/yaml/), [MSBuild properties](reference/msbuild-properties/), [diagnostics](reference/diagnostics/) and [troubleshooting](troubleshooting/).

## Glossary

[Section titled “Glossary”](#glossary)

The docs use these terms throughout.

| Term                    | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Options type**        | A class or record whose instance holds one configuration section’s values, read by code through `IOptions<T>`.                                                                                                       |
| **Section**             | The part of the application’s configuration an options type is read from, named by its **section path** (for example `Http:Retry`). An options type has exactly one section.                                         |
| **Declaration**         | Marking an options type with its section, on the type itself (`[Optionary]`) or, for a type you don’t own, on the assembly (`[assembly: Optionary<T>]`). A rejected declaration is reported and contributes nothing. |
| **Key style**           | How a declaration spells the keys of its options type and everything nested in it. An explicit key name on a member always wins.                                                                                     |
| **Registration method** | The method generated into each assembly that has declarations, which registers that assembly’s options types with the options pipeline. It exists even when every declaration was rejected.                          |
| **Fragment**            | The description of one section’s shape that an assembly carries with it, so that projects referencing the assembly can learn the section without running its code.                                                   |
| **Library schema**      | The file a library packs, describing only its own sections. It is permissive.                                                                                                                                        |
| **Host**                | A project whose build combines its own fragments with those of everything it references: applications and test projects.                                                                                             |
| **Application schema**  | The one file a host’s build writes, covering every section it can see plus the common appsettings keys. It is strict: unknown keys in a section are flagged, ignoring case.                                          |
| **Merge**               | Producing the application schema from fragments. The same fragments always give the same file, whatever order the references come in.                                                                                |

## Origins

[Section titled “Origins”](#origins)

Optionary started as the configuration schema and binding feature of [Dovetail](https://github.com/RocketSurgeonsGuild/Dovetail). It was imported from Dovetail at commit [`3f512a33b0`](https://github.com/RocketSurgeonsGuild/Dovetail/commit/3f512a33b0) and renamed; it doesn’t depend on Dovetail and works without it.

# Getting started

> Add Optionary, declare an options type, register it, and get completion for its section in appsettings files.

## Requirements

[Section titled “Requirements”](#requirements)

* A project targeting `net10.0` or `net11.0`.
* C# 12 or later. With an older `LangVersion` the generator binds nothing and reports [`OPT0001`](../reference/diagnostics/#opt0001).
* A compiler that can load Roslyn 5.0 or later analyzers (the .NET 10 SDK or later). With an older one, the generator isn’t loaded and the build fails with [`OPT1001`](../reference/diagnostics/#opt1001).

## Add the package

[Section titled “Add the package”](#add-the-package)

```sh
dotnet add package Optionary
```

The package carries the runtime library, the source generator and the MSBuild targets that write the schema. Its build assets flow transitively, so a project that references a library built with Optionary merges that library’s fragments into its own application schema.

## Declare an options type

[Section titled “Declare an options type”](#declare-an-options-type)

Put `[Optionary]` on the class (or record) that holds the section’s values:

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using Optionary;


namespace MyApp;


/// <summary>Options for the greetings this application prints.</summary>
[Optionary] // section "Greetings": the type name without its "Options" suffix
public sealed class GreetingsOptions
{
    /// <summary>The text that comes before the name.</summary>
    public string Message { get; set; } = "Hello";


    /// <summary>How many times the greeting is said.</summary>
    [Range(1, 5)]
    public int Repeat { get; set; } = 1;
}
```

The [declarations](../guides/declarations/) guide covers explicit section paths, the assembly form for types you don’t own, and the other attribute properties.

## Register it

[Section titled “Register it”](#register-it)

The generator writes a **registration method** into the assembly: an internal extension method, `AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions()`, in a class named `OptionaryConfigurationOptions` in the project’s `RootNamespace`. Call it once on the service collection:

```csharp
using MyApp; // the project's RootNamespace, where the registration method lives


var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions();
```

Then read the options the usual way, through `IOptions<GreetingsOptions>`, `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` or `IOptionsMonitor<T>`:

```csharp
public sealed class Greeter(IOptions<GreetingsOptions> options)
{
    public string Greet(string name) => $"{options.Value.Message}, {name}";
}
```

The binder is generated code, so nothing here uses reflection. A library calls its own registration method from a public extension method instead; see [registering from a library](../guides/registering-from-a-library/).

## Write the configuration

[Section titled “Write the configuration”](#write-the-configuration)

appsettings.json

```json
{
    "Greetings": {
        "Message": "Howdy",
        "Repeat": 2
    }
}
```

## Point your editor at the schema

[Section titled “Point your editor at the schema”](#point-your-editor-at-the-schema)

Build the project once. An application or test project is a **host**, and its build writes the **application schema** to `obj/appsettings.schema.json`, merged from its own fragments and those of every assembly it references.

* **Visual Studio** picks it up for `appsettings*.json` with no setup.
* **VS Code** needs a mapping in `.vscode/settings.json`, which Optionary can write for you: set `<OptionaryScaffoldEditorSettings>true</OptionaryScaffoldEditorSettings>`.
* **Rider** needs a JSON Schema mapping.

[Schema and editors](../guides/schema-and-editors/) has the details for each.

# Binding and validation

> The reflection-free binder Optionary generates, the types it supports, how options are registered and validated, and where it deliberately differs from Microsoft's binding generator.

Every declared options type is created and bound by generated code and registered through an `IOptionsFactory<T>`. Nothing uses reflection, so registration is trimming and Native AOT safe, and your own `Configure<T>`, `PostConfigure<T>` and validators still run on the created instance, whenever they were registered.

## The generated binder

[Section titled “The generated binder”](#the-generated-binder)

Optionary doesn’t call Microsoft’s configuration binding source generator: a source generator never sees another generator’s output, so calls in Optionary’s own generated code would not be intercepted. Instead it **ports** that generator (the parser, the type specifications and the emitter from dotnet/runtime’s `Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder/gen`, MIT), with both its version 10 and version 11 rules.

The rules follow the **major version of `Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Binder`** the project references, not its target framework, because a `net10.0` application can reference Binder 11. A project that references no Binder gets the version 11 rules.

### Binder 10 and Binder 11

[Section titled “Binder 10 and Binder 11”](#binder-10-and-binder-11)

| Case                                           | Binder 10              | Binder 11                    |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `Nullable<T>` set to `""`                      | value kept             | `null`                       |
| String or object constructor parameter missing | throws                 | `null`                       |
| Value-type constructor parameter set to `""`   | default                | throws                       |
| Nullable or reference-type parameter missing   | throws                 | `null` (structs still throw) |
| Parameter with a default, set to null          | `null`                 | the default                  |
| Properties bound through the constructor       | bound again afterwards | not bound again              |
| `[ConfigurationIgnore]`                        | ignored                | honoured, in the schema too  |

The same data is bound three ways in the parity tests (Microsoft’s generator, the reflection binder and Optionary’s) on both versions.

### Where Optionary differs from Microsoft’s generator, on purpose

[Section titled “Where Optionary differs from Microsoft’s generator, on purpose”](#where-optionary-differs-from-microsofts-generator-on-purpose)

1. **Object-initializer types.** Microsoft’s generator never sets `init`-only members of a type with a parameterless constructor, and can’t create a type with `required` members (CS9035). Optionary creates them with an object initializer, then binds the rest. A missing key keeps the member’s own initial value, as the reflection binder does; a `required` member with no value gets `default`.
2. **`required` members that can’t be bound** (an unsupported type, or `[ConfigurationIgnore]`) are set to `default!`, so the generated code compiles. [`OPT0004`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0004) reports the member.
3. **Empty sections still produce an instance.** `Get<T>()` returns `null` for a missing section, but `IOptions<T>.Value` can’t be `null`. A missing required constructor parameter throws the first time the options are read.
4. **No `NotSupportedException`s**, and no `BindNonPublicProperties`.
5. **Self-expanding generics**, such as `class Node<T> { Node<Node<T>> Next; }`, are treated as unsupported past a nesting depth of 10 or 1,000 types, instead of making the analysis run forever. The schema reports [`OPT0007`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0007) for the same graphs.

Microsoft’s own quirks are kept: a positional record’s extra `init`-only property is set to `default` when its key is missing, overriding its initializer, and Binder 10 binds constructor-bound collections twice.

Registration also differs from `services.Configure<T>(section)`: the configuration’s reload token feeds `IOptionsMonitor<T>` through one change token source per type, and the `IConfiguration` is resolved from the container when the options are first created, not captured at registration.

## Supported types

[Section titled “Supported types”](#supported-types)

The binder follows Microsoft’s binding generator, not the JSON serializer:

* `string`, `bool`, every numeric type (including `Half`, `Int128` and `UInt128`), `char`, enums (any casing), `TimeSpan`, `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset`, `DateOnly`, `TimeOnly`, `Guid`, `Version`, `Uri`, `CultureInfo` and `byte[]`;
* `Nullable<T>` of those;
* nested classes, structs and records, and recursive types (the schema uses `$ref`);
* arrays, lists, sets and the other collection types the binder supports, and dictionaries with string, enum or integer keys;
* `object` and `IConfigurationSection`, which accept any value.

A type with a `[TypeConverter]` is described as an object, because the binder ignores converters. A member the binder can’t bind is left out of both the schema and the binder, with warning [`OPT0004`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0004). `[ConfigurationKeyName]` renames a key, and from Binder 11 `[ConfigurationIgnore]` leaves a member out.

## Records and other immutable types

[Section titled “Records and other immutable types”](#records-and-other-immutable-types)

Types the options pipeline can’t create itself (constructor parameters, `init`-only or `required` members) are registered like any other: the generated code builds the instance from the section, and your `Configure<T>` and validators still run on it.

```csharp
[Optionary]
public sealed record FarewellOptions(string Message, [property: Range(0, 5)] int Exclamations);
```

## How options are registered

[Section titled “How options are registered”](#how-options-are-registered)

The [registration method](../registering-from-a-library/) calls one public method per options type, `OptionaryServiceCollectionExtensions.AddOptionaryOptions<TOptions>`, passing the create function it generated for the type. It is also yours to call, for example for a type declared with `RegisterOptions = false`.

### Registering by hand

[Section titled “Registering by hand”](#registering-by-hand)

```csharp
services.AddOptionaryOptions<GreetingsOptions>("Greetings", static configuration => new GreetingsOptions
{
    Message = configuration["Message"] ?? "Hello",
});
```

`AddOptionaryOptions<TOptions>(this IServiceCollection services, string sectionPath, Func<IConfiguration, TOptions> create)` returns the `OptionsBuilder<TOptions>`, so `Validate` and `ValidateOnStart()` chain as usual.

* The configuration is the application’s complete `IConfiguration`, resolved from the service provider when the options are first created. `create` receives its section at `sectionPath` (such as `Http:Retry`). An empty path throws.
* A change token source watches the configuration, so `IOptionsMonitor<T>` and `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` see reloads.
* The call registers an `IOptionsFactory<T>` with `TryAdd`: the first registration for a type wins and later calls are ignored. A factory your application registers itself wins over Optionary’s, and `create` is never called for that type.
* The factory derives from `OptionsFactory<T>`, so configure and post-configure actions and validators still run on the instance `create` returns. On .NET 11, don’t give such a type asynchronous validators: they fail synchronous validation through a derived factory.

There is one overload because everything is created through generated code. To bind a type with reflection, use Microsoft’s `Configure<T>(IConfiguration)` or `AddOptions<T>().Bind(...)` yourself.

### Named options

[Section titled “Named options”](#named-options)

Optionary registers the default options only. Reading any other name, such as `IOptionsMonitor<T>.Get("tenant-a")`, throws an `InvalidOperationException` naming the type and the options name.

## Validation

[Section titled “Validation”](#validation)

Optionary never turns on `ValidateDataAnnotations`. `[Range]`, `[MinLength]` and the other annotations describe the [schema](../schema-and-editors/), which is how editors flag a bad value; they are not enforced at run time.

To enforce rules, write an `[OptionsValidator]` class, the options validation source generator from `Microsoft.Extensions.Options`:

```csharp
[OptionsValidator]
public sealed partial class GreetingsOptionsValidator : IValidateOptions<GreetingsOptions>;
```

The registration method registers every such validator in the assembly for the options types it registers, with `TryAddEnumerable`, so it never duplicates one you added yourself. Set `ValidateOnStart = true` on the declaration and a bad configuration fails the host at startup.

### ZeroAlloc.Validation

[Section titled “ZeroAlloc.Validation”](#zeroallocvalidation)

With [ZeroAlloc.Validation](https://validation.zeroalloc.net/docs/options) and `ZeroAlloc.Validation.Options` referenced, mark the options type `[Validate]` instead: the registration method calls the `ValidateWithZeroAlloc()` overload that ZeroAlloc.Validation generates for it.

* It applies to `[Validate]` classes of the same assembly that aren’t private or protected (nor nested in a type that is). `ZeroAllocGeneratedAccessibility=Internal` is honoured.
* A type with an asynchronous rule isn’t validated this way, because options validation is synchronous; it is reported with [`OPT0012`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0012).
* Set `OptionaryZeroAllocValidation` to `false` to leave ZeroAlloc.Validation’s registrations to the project.

# Declarations

> Mark an options type with its section, on the type or on the assembly, and how the section path is derived.

A **declaration** marks an **options type** with its **section**. There are two forms, and a type has exactly one section, so it is declared once.

## On the type: `[Optionary]`

[Section titled “On the type: \[Optionary\]”](#on-the-type-optionary)

Put `[Optionary]` on a class or record you own:

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel;
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using Optionary;


/// <summary>Options for the greetings this library prints.</summary>
[Optionary]
public sealed class GreetingsOptions
{
    /// <summary>What the greeting says before the name.</summary>
    [Description("The text that comes before the name, e.g. \"Hello\".")]
    public string Message { get; set; } = "Hello";


    /// <summary>How many times the greeting is said.</summary>
    [Range(1, 5)]
    public int Repeat { get; set; } = 1;
}
```

Records and other immutable types work too; see [binding](../binding/#records-and-other-immutable-types):

```csharp
[Optionary]
public sealed record FarewellOptions(string Message, [property: Range(0, 5)] int Exclamations);
```

`[Optionary]` can’t be repeated on a type.

## On the assembly: `[assembly: Optionary<T>]`

[Section titled “On the assembly: \[assembly: Optionary\<T>\]”](#on-the-assembly-assembly-optionaryt)

To declare a type you don’t own, use the generic attribute on the assembly. This declares `HostOptions` under `Hosting`:

```csharp
[assembly: Optionary<HostOptions>("Hosting")]
```

Repeat the attribute for each type. Descriptions for a type from a package come from the XML documentation file that ships with the package, when there is one (see `OptionaryReferenceDocumentation` in the [MSBuild reference](../../reference/msbuild-properties/)).

## The section path

[Section titled “The section path”](#the-section-path)

| Declaration                           | Section path                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `[Optionary]`                         | The type name with one `Configuration`, `Settings`, `Options` or `Config` suffix removed, spelled in the declaration’s [key style](../key-styles/): `GreetingsOptions` is `Greetings`. |
| `[Optionary("Http:Retry")]`           | The path you give, used as written. `:` nests sections.                                                                                                                                |
| `[assembly: Optionary<T>]`            | The same rule as the class form, applied to `T`.                                                                                                                                       |
| `[assembly: Optionary<T>("Hosting")]` | The path you give.                                                                                                                                                                     |

* There is no prefix: a library’s sections sit at the configuration root unless you give a path.
* Configuration keys ignore case, so `Greetings` and `greetings` are the same section.
* The suffix is matched case-sensitively, and only one is removed.
* A path that is empty, has an empty segment (`A::B`), or a type name that would be empty without its suffix (a class called `Options`) is rejected with [`OPT0003`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0003). Give it a path.

## What can be declared

[Section titled “What can be declared”](#what-can-be-declared)

An options type is a class or record class that configuration can create. These are rejected with [`OPT0002`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0002): interfaces, static and abstract classes, structs, enums, open generic types and collections. A type that can’t be created from configuration (no public constructor, several public constructors with parameters and none without, or a constructor parameter that matches no property) is rejected with [`OPT0006`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0006).

A rejected declaration is reported and contributes nothing: no fragment and no registration. The assembly still gets its [registration method](../registering-from-a-library/).

## One section per type

[Section titled “One section per type”](#one-section-per-type)

* `[Optionary]` and `[assembly: Optionary<T>]` for the same type is an error, [`OPT0010`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0010), reported on the assembly attribute. The class declaration is the one that produces the fragment and the registration; the assembly attribute produces nothing.
* Naming the same `T` in two assembly attributes is `OPT0010` too.

At run time each assembly reads only its own sections from the application’s complete `IConfiguration`. Optionary doesn’t order, de-duplicate or merge sections at run time; the registration method registers an assembly’s types by section path, then type name, and the standard options pipeline does the rest.

## Attribute properties

[Section titled “Attribute properties”](#attribute-properties)

Both forms have the same members.

| Member            | Default     | Effect                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Section`         | derived     | The section path, from the constructor argument. Left out, it is derived from the type name.                                                             |
| `KeyStyle`        | `Undefined` | How keys are spelled. See [key styles](../key-styles/).                                                                                                  |
| `RegisterOptions` | `true`      | `false` only describes the section in the schema. Nothing is registered, so you bind the type yourself (see [binding](../binding/#registering-by-hand)). |
| `ValidateOnStart` | `false`     | Validates the options when the host starts, instead of the first time they are read.                                                                     |

The attributes are `[Conditional("CodeGeneration")]`: the generator reads them from source, and they never reach the compiled assembly’s metadata.

# Key styles

> Spell the keys of an options type as declared, or in Pascal, camel, dash or underscore case.

A declaration’s **key style** picks how the keys of its options type, and of everything nested in it, are spelled. It is set per declaration with `KeyStyle`, on `[Optionary]` and on `[assembly: Optionary<T>]`. There is no assembly-wide or MSBuild default.

```csharp
[Optionary(KeyStyle = ConfigurationKeyStyle.Underscore)]
public class HttpClientOptions // section "http_client"
{
    public int MaxFileSizeMb { get; set; } // key "max_file_size_mb"
    public RetryPolicy Retry { get; set; } = new(); // "retry:max_attempts" through RetryPolicy.MaxAttempts
}
```

## The five styles

[Section titled “The five styles”](#the-five-styles)

| `ConfigurationKeyStyle` | The key is                                           | `MaxFileSizeMb`    | `HTTPServer`  | `HttpClientOptions` section |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------- | --------------------------- |
| `Undefined` (default)   | The declared name exactly as written.                | `MaxFileSizeMb`    | `HTTPServer`  | `HttpClient`                |
| `Pascal`                | The declared name with its first letter upper-cased. | `MaxFileSizeMb`    | `HTTPServer`  | `HttpClient`                |
| `Camel`                 | Lower camel case (`JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase`).     | `maxFileSizeMb`    | `httpServer`  | `httpClient`                |
| `Dash`                  | Lower-case words joined with `-` (`KebabCaseLower`). | `max-file-size-mb` | `http-server` | `http-client`               |
| `Underscore`            | Lower-case words joined with `_` (`SnakeCaseLower`). | `max_file_size_mb` | `http_server` | `http_client`               |

## What the style changes

[Section titled “What the style changes”](#what-the-style-changes)

* **`Undefined` respells nothing.** The binder, the schema’s keys and the derived section path use the names as declared. Configuration keys ignore case, so `maxfilesizemb`, `MaxFileSizeMb` and `MAXFILESIZEMB` are the same key. Dashes and underscores are other characters, though: `max-file-size-mb` does not match `MaxFileSizeMb`.
* **`Pascal` is explicit.** C# property names already start in upper case, so for them `Undefined` and `Pascal` are the same. They differ for a member declared as `myKey`: it stays `myKey` under `Undefined` and becomes `MyKey` under `Pascal`.
* **What it covers.** The key of every bound property and constructor parameter of the options type and of every object type nested in it, in lists and dictionary values too. The generated binder reads those keys, and the schema uses them for its properties, its case-insensitive twins and the strict key check.
* **What it leaves alone.** Dictionary keys, enum values and other data are never restyled, and neither is an explicit section path: `"Http:Retry"` is used as written.
* **Word splitting** is `System.Text.Json`’s. `HTTPServer` becomes `httpServer`, `http-server` and `http_server`; `Http2Enabled` becomes `http2Enabled`, `http2-enabled` and `http2_enabled`.
* **An explicit key name always wins.** `[ConfigurationKeyName]` is used verbatim, in every style.
* **Derived section paths follow the style**, after the suffix is removed: `HttpClientOptions` is `HttpClient`, `httpClient`, `http-client` and `http_client`.

### Case versus letters

[Section titled “Case versus letters”](#case-versus-letters)

Because keys ignore case, `Camel` against `Undefined` or `Pascal` only changes the spelling the schema suggests: `maxFileSizeMb` and `MaxFileSizeMb` bind the same value. `Dash` and `Underscore` change the characters the binder reads: a value written as `MaxFileSizeMb` no longer binds (`max-file-size-mb` or `max_file_size_mb` does), and the schema only accepts those keys, in any case.

## One spelling per type

[Section titled “One spelling per type”](#one-spelling-per-type)

The binder is generated once for each type. A type reached from sections that spell its keys differently, such as a `RetryOptions` used by a camel section and a dash section, can’t be bound correctly for both. The later declaration is reported as [`OPT0011`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0011) and contributes nothing.

* The comparison is of the effective keys, not the style names. `Undefined` and `Pascal` don’t conflict on ordinary names, which spell the same keys, but do on a member declared in lower case.
* Fix it by using the same `KeyStyle` for every section that reaches the type, or by giving the shared type `[ConfigurationKeyName]` attributes. A type whose keys don’t depend on the style isn’t a conflict.
* Declarations with `RegisterOptions = false` bind nothing, so they can’t conflict.

# Registering from a library

> The registration method Optionary generates into every assembly, its contract, and how a library exposes it.

Optionary generates a **registration method** into every assembly that uses the `[Optionary]` attribute. It registers that assembly’s options types with the options pipeline. It is internal on purpose, so a library calls it from its own public extension method and the method never becomes part of the library’s public API.

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;


namespace Contoso.Greetings; // the library's RootNamespace


public static class GreetingsServiceCollectionExtensions
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddGreetings(this IServiceCollection services)
    {
        services.AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions(); // generated, internal, in Contoso.Greetings
        services.AddSingleton<Greeter>();
        return services;
    }
}
```

An application does the same from its own startup code: see [getting started](../../getting-started/#register-it).

## The contract

[Section titled “The contract”](#the-contract)

The method’s name, its class, its signature and the rules below are public API. They change only in a major version, and host frameworks rely on them: Dovetail, for one, calls the method from a joint it generates when it finds `[Optionary]` declarations.

```csharp
namespace <RootNamespace>;


[global::System.CodeDom.Compiler.GeneratedCode("Optionary", "<version>")]
internal static class OptionaryConfigurationOptions
{
    internal static global::Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.IServiceCollection AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions(
        this global::Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.IServiceCollection services);
}
```

* **File.** The hint name is `Optionary.Options.g.cs`.

* **Always emitted when the attribute type is present.** The method exists in every compilation where `Optionary.OptionaryAttribute` resolves to the type in the assembly named `Optionary`, so a call to it always compiles:

  * with no declarations at all;
  * when every declaration was rejected;
  * when every declaration has `RegisterOptions = false`;
  * when the C# version is older than 12: the body is empty and [`OPT0001`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0001) is reported.

  A class of your own named `Optionary.OptionaryAttribute` in another assembly doesn’t count, and nothing is emitted for it.

* **The `RootNamespace` rule.** The class goes in the project’s `RootNamespace` build property, used verbatim. When `RootNamespace` is missing, empty or whitespace, the class is in the global namespace. Optionary’s build assets make `RootNamespace` visible to the generator.

* **What it registers.** One `AddOptionaryOptions<T>(services, "<section path>", create)` call per registered options type, ordered by section path (ignoring case, then ordinal) and then type name. A declaration with `ValidateOnStart = true` gets `ValidateOnStart()`, and a `[Validate]` type gets `ValidateWithZeroAlloc()` (see [validation](../binding/#validation)). Then every `[OptionsValidator]` class of the assembly for those types, with `TryAddEnumerable`.

* **Repeat calls are harmless.** Every registration is a `TryAdd` or `TryAddEnumerable`, so a library’s own `AddGreetings()` and a host framework can both call it.

* **It returns `services`**, for chaining.

## Two assemblies with the same `RootNamespace`

[Section titled “Two assemblies with the same RootNamespace”](#two-assemblies-with-the-same-rootnamespace)

Each assembly’s class is internal, so two assemblies normally don’t see each other’s. If one has `InternalsVisibleTo` the other and both have the same `RootNamespace`, the consumer gets warning CS0436 and the definition in its own source wins. Give the projects distinct `RootNamespace`s.

## If the method is missing

[Section titled “If the method is missing”](#if-the-method-is-missing)

A call to `AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions` that doesn’t compile (CS1061, CS0234 or CS0103) usually means Optionary’s build assets are excluded: the generator still runs, but without `RootNamespace`, so the method is in the global namespace. See [troubleshooting](../../troubleshooting/).

# Schema and editors

> Fragments, the library schema, the merged application schema, and how Visual Studio, VS Code and Rider use it.

Every application built with Optionary gets one JSON Schema for its configuration, merged from the declarations of every assembly it references. Editors use it to complete section and key names in `appsettings.json`, YAML and TOML files, to show the documentation you wrote on the options types, and to flag unknown keys and out-of-range values.

## Fragments

[Section titled “Fragments”](#fragments)

The generator embeds one **fragment** per section in the assembly:

```csharp
[assembly: AssemblyMetadata("Optionary.Schema.v1:<section path>", "<JSON Schema of the section's value>")]
```

Each fragment is a Draft-07 schema of the section’s value, with every object type described once under `definitions`. Every key also has a case-insensitive `patternProperties` twin with the same schema, so `retries: 99` is checked even when written as `Retries`.

Hand-written fragments in the same format are supported: a library whose section isn’t described by an options type can add the attribute itself, and it is merged like any other. Only the `Optionary.Schema.v1:` prefix is read.

### Annotations that reach the schema

[Section titled “Annotations that reach the schema”](#annotations-that-reach-the-schema)

| Source                                      | Schema                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `[Description]`, else the XML `<summary>`   | `description`. For a record parameter, its `<param>`.     |
| `[Range]`, length attributes                | `minimum`/`maximum`, `minLength`/`maxLength`, item counts |
| `[RegularExpression]`                       | `pattern`, when the expression can be anchored            |
| `[Url]`, `[EmailAddress]`                   | `format`                                                  |
| `[Obsolete]`                                | `deprecated` and a deprecation message                    |
| A constant initializer or parameter default | `default`, except an empty string                         |

* Ranges and defaults are also written into the description, since editors don’t show them.
* The XML summary is read from source whether or not `GenerateDocumentationFile` is on. `<inheritdoc />` and `<include>` produce no description.
* Annotations JSON Schema can’t express are dropped with [`OPT0008`](../../reference/diagnostics/#opt0008).
* Fragments are permissive: nothing is `required` unless `OptionarySchemaRequired` is `true`, which marks `required` members, `[Required]` properties and value-type constructor parameters without defaults.

## The library schema

[Section titled “The library schema”](#the-library-schema)

Every project that isn’t a host (a library) writes its own fragments to `$(IntermediateOutputPath)ConfigurationSchema.json` and packs it at the NuGet package root. This **library schema** is permissive and rooted at the configuration root, the layout Aspire’s packages use, so Visual Studio and other tools that understand it can read it. A library that targets several frameworks writes one per framework and packs the first one’s. A library with no sections writes nothing.

## The application schema

[Section titled “The application schema”](#the-application-schema)

A **host** is a test project (`IsTestProject`) or an application (`OutputType` `Exe` or `WinExe`, or an Android application). Set `OptionarySchemaHost` to `true` or `false` to override the detection; a host framework can set it from its own application detection.

A host **merges** its own fragments and those of every referenced assembly into `$(BaseIntermediateOutputPath)appsettings.schema.json`, normally `obj/appsettings.schema.json`.

* **Stable path.** Editors can point at it and the setting can be checked in. A host that targets several frameworks writes it from its first target framework, and `$(IntermediateOutputPath)appsettings.schema.json` (for example `obj/Debug/net10.0/`) from the others.
* **Copied and published.** It is copied to `$(OutDir)` next to `appsettings.json` and published as `appsettings.schema.json`. A project that references the host (a test project referencing an application) doesn’t get a second copy. Set `OptionarySchemaCopyToOutput` to `false` to keep it in `obj/` only, for hosts that embed their configuration (MAUI, Uno).
* **No collisions.** A hand-made `appsettings.schema.json` (Web SDK content, or one from a reference) is removed from the publish items so it doesn’t collide with the generated one (NETSDK1152).
* **Strict.** Each Optionary section, and the object types it uses, accepts only its own keys. The check is a case-insensitive `propertyNames` pattern rather than `additionalProperties: false`, so `message` is accepted and `Mesage` is flagged, with an error that lists the known keys. The root, parents shared between sections, dictionaries and sections declared by more than one assembly stay open. `OptionarySchemaStrict=false` turns the check off.
* **Includes SchemaStore.** SchemaStore’s `appsettings.json` schema is embedded, not referenced, so `Logging`, `Kestrel` and `ConnectionStrings` complete too, online or offline. The copy ships with Optionary (Apache-2.0). `OptionarySchemaIncludeSchemaStore=false` leaves it out.
* **Deterministic.** Section paths compare ignoring case. When fragments spell a section or key differently, the ordinal-smallest spelling is shown. A section several assemblies declare is merged into one object. The same fragments always give a byte-identical file, whatever order the references come in.

Note

Editors flag a quoted number such as `"Timeout": "30"` as the wrong type, although the binder accepts it. The schema stays strict about types so that ranges are always checked.

The build target runs after `CoreCompile`, skips design-time builds and writes only when its inputs change. Merging runs in a compiled MSBuild task that reads fragments with `System.Reflection.Metadata`: no assembly is loaded, and nothing is embedded in your application. All the properties are in the [MSBuild reference](../../reference/msbuild-properties/).

## Visual Studio

[Section titled “Visual Studio”](#visual-studio)

Visual Studio’s JSON editor reads schemas from `JsonSchemaSegment` items. Optionary adds them with the file pattern `appsettings\..*json`, the one Aspire’s packages use:

* a segment for the host’s `obj/appsettings.schema.json`;
* a segment for each referenced package that ships a `ConfigurationSchema.json` at its root, as libraries built with Optionary do. A package that declares its own segment for the file (Aspire’s client packages do) is skipped, so completions aren’t doubled. Project references need none: their fragments are in the host’s file.

Nothing needs configuring. The items are added after `ResolveAssemblyReferences`, so they exist in the design-time builds Visual Studio runs when it loads the project. `OptionarySchemaVisualStudio=false` turns the segments off and keeps the schema files. If completion doesn’t appear after the first build, close and reopen the file.

Note

Segments only affect Visual Studio’s JSON editor; YAML and TOML files get nothing from them. Optionary’s tests check the items MSBuild produces, including in a design-time build, but whether Visual Studio reads items a target adds, and how it merges two segments that describe the same section, has not been verified in Visual Studio itself.

## Visual Studio Code

[Section titled “Visual Studio Code”](#visual-studio-code)

VS Code needs one mapping per file type: its JSON support reads `json.schemas`, and the YAML (Red Hat) and Even Better TOML extensions read `yaml.schemas` and `evenBetterToml.schema.associations`. Put them in `.vscode/settings.json`:

```jsonc
{
    "json.schemas": [
        {
            "fileMatch": ["/MyApp/appsettings*.json"],
            "url": "./MyApp/obj/appsettings.schema.json",
        },
    ],
    "yaml.schemas": {
        "./MyApp/obj/appsettings.schema.json": ["MyApp/appsettings*.yaml", "MyApp/appsettings*.yml"],
    },
    "evenBetterToml.schema.associations": {
        "^.+/MyApp/appsettings.*\\.toml$": "./MyApp/obj/appsettings.schema.json",
    },
}
```

* **JSON** reports unknown keys, completes the canonical names and shows descriptions on hover.
* **YAML** does the same. Its `fileMatch` globs don’t match files under a dot-folder.
* **TOML** needs the explicit association: Even Better TOML can’t use the SchemaStore catalog, and it reports an unknown key on the table header rather than on the key. It ignores `deprecated`.

### Let Optionary write the settings

[Section titled “Let Optionary write the settings”](#let-optionary-write-the-settings)

Set `OptionaryScaffoldEditorSettings` in the application’s project file:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <OptionaryScaffoldEditorSettings>true</OptionaryScaffoldEditorSettings>
</PropertyGroup>
```

On build, Optionary creates or updates **only its own** entries in `.vscode/settings.json` (`json.schemas`, `yaml.schemas` and `evenBetterToml.schema.associations`), pointing at the host’s `obj/appsettings.schema.json`.

* Comments, trailing commas, indentation, line endings and a byte-order mark are preserved. Other settings and other entries are untouched, and when the mappings are already there the file isn’t rewritten.
* Each host gets entries of its own, keyed by its schema path, so several applications can share one file. An entry that already maps the host’s schema only gets what is missing. If you move a project, delete its old entries by hand.
* The file goes in the nearest ancestor of the project that contains a `.git` entry, or the project folder when there is none. `OptionaryEditorSettingsDirectory` picks another folder (relative to the project); it must contain the project, because VS Code resolves the schema path relative to the folder it opened.
* Only hosts write it, once per build (from the first target framework), never in design-time builds, and not when `OptionarySchema` is `false`.
* A file Optionary can’t update safely (not valid JSON with comments, not UTF-8, an unexpected shape, read-only) is left alone, and the build warns with the entries to paste.
* Optionary never adds `$schema` keys or `# yaml-language-server` modelines to your configuration files.

It is off by default because it edits a file that is probably checked in. Existing mappings keep working across Optionary versions, since entries are matched by schema path.

## JetBrains Rider

[Section titled “JetBrains Rider”](#jetbrains-rider)

Rider uses its own JSON Schema mappings:

1. Open **Settings | Languages & Frameworks | Schemas and DTDs | JSON Schema Mappings**.
2. Add a mapping, choose `obj/appsettings.schema.json` as the schema file, set the version to Draft 7, and add the application’s `appsettings*.json` files.
3. Rider applies JSON Schema mappings to YAML files too; add the `appsettings*.yaml` files the same way.

## Other editors

[Section titled “Other editors”](#other-editors)

* **yaml-language-server** reads a `yaml.schemas` setting like VS Code’s, or a `# yaml-language-server: $schema=...` modeline in the file.
* **Taplo** takes the schema from `.taplo.toml`.

## When completion doesn’t work

[Section titled “When completion doesn’t work”](#when-completion-doesnt-work)

* **No completion at all.** Build the project: the file is written after compilation. Check that the mapping’s path is relative to the folder the editor opened, and that the file name matches `appsettings*`.
* **A key is flagged as unknown.** Check its spelling against the options type. Set `OptionarySchemaStrict` to `false` to stop the check.
* **A section is missing.** The application schema only covers assemblies the host references. Check the options type is declared and the declaration wasn’t rejected (look for `OPT` diagnostics).
* **Quoted numbers are flagged.** Write the number without quotes.

# YAML provider

> Optionary.Configuration.Yaml, a YAML configuration provider for Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.

`Optionary.Configuration.Yaml` is a YAML configuration provider for `Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration`, built on YamlDotNet. It is its own package and doesn’t depend on `Optionary`: you can use it without declarations or schemas, and `Optionary` doesn’t need it. It is trimming and Native AOT compatible.

```sh
dotnet add package Optionary.Configuration.Yaml
```

## Adding YAML files

[Section titled “Adding YAML files”](#adding-yaml-files)

```csharp
using Optionary.Configuration.Yaml;


var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Configuration
    .AddYamlFile("appsettings.yaml", optional: true, reloadOnChange: true)
    .AddYamlFile($"appsettings.{builder.Environment.EnvironmentName}.yaml", optional: true, reloadOnChange: true);
```

appsettings.yaml

```yaml
Greetings:
    Message: Howdy
    Repeat: 2
    Recipients:
        - Ada
        - Grace
```

| Method                                                                 | Adds                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AddYamlFile(path)`                                                    | A required file, relative to the builder’s base path.           |
| `AddYamlFile(path, optional)`                                          | A file that may be missing.                                     |
| `AddYamlFile(path, optional, reloadOnChange)`                          | The same, reloaded when the file changes.                       |
| `AddYamlFile(IFileProvider? provider, path, optional, reloadOnChange)` | A file read through the given file provider.                    |
| `AddYamlFile(Action<YamlConfigurationSource> configureSource)`         | A source you configure yourself.                                |
| `AddYamlStream(Stream stream)`                                         | YAML read once from a stream, for example an embedded resource. |

## How YAML maps to configuration

[Section titled “How YAML maps to configuration”](#how-yaml-maps-to-configuration)

* Mappings become nested keys joined with `:`, so `Greetings: { Message: Howdy }` is `Greetings:Message`.
* Sequences become indexed keys: `Greetings:Recipients:0`, `Greetings:Recipients:1`.
* A plain (unquoted) `~`, `null`, `Null` or `NULL` is a null value. Quote it to keep the text.
* Keys ignore case, as everywhere in configuration, so a key that appears twice in any casing is a `FormatException`.
* Only the first document of a multi-document file is read, and its root must be a mapping. YAML that doesn’t parse is a `FormatException` with YamlDotNet’s message.

## Schemas for YAML files

[Section titled “Schemas for YAML files”](#schemas-for-yaml-files)

The [application schema](../schema-and-editors/) describes YAML files as well as JSON ones: map `appsettings*.yaml` to it in your editor, or let `OptionaryScaffoldEditorSettings` write the VS Code mapping.

## With Dovetail

[Section titled “With Dovetail”](#with-dovetail)

The package’s `build/Optionary.Configuration.Yaml.targets` declares three Dovetail joint templates, so a Dovetail application gets its YAML files loaded without any code. Only Dovetail reads `DovetailTemplate` items, and only in a project that runs Dovetail’s generator and references this package; without Dovetail they do nothing, and nothing extra is compiled.

| `DovetailTemplate`  | Generated joint                                 | What it adds                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `YamlJoint`         | `YamlJoint` (`IConfigurationJoint`)             | `appsettings.yaml`, `appsettings.{Environment}.yaml`, the same named after the application, and the `.local` overrides, each also as `.yml`, from the configuration’s file provider. |
| `YamlBrowserJoint`  | `YamlBrowserJoint` (`IConfigurationAsyncJoint`) | The same files in the browser (WebAssembly), downloaded from the application’s base address.                                                                                         |
| `YamlEmbeddedJoint` | `YamlEmbeddedJoint` (`IConfigurationJoint`)     | The YAML files of hosts that embed their configuration in the assembly (MAUI, Uno), read with `AddYamlStream`.                                                                       |

* Each item has `Package="Optionary.Configuration.Yaml"` and `OutputPrefix="OptionaryYaml"`. The joints are generated as internal classes in the namespace `Optionary.Configuration.Yaml`, and each adds its files once even when a test project imports the application’s copy as well as its own.
* The items are declared only in applications (`OutputType` `Exe` or `WinExe`, or an Android application) and test projects (`IsTestProject`). A joint compiled into a library would be exported to every application that references it, so libraries never get one, and each application gets exactly one of each.
* The targets also add a `BlazorConfigurationFile` assembly metadata entry listing `wwwroot/appsettings*.yml` and `wwwroot/appsettings*.yaml`, which the browser joint uses to know which files to download.

# Diagnostics

> The OPT diagnostics the generator and the build report, and how to fix each.

The generator reports `OPT0001` to `OPT0012`, in the `Optionary` category. `OPT1001` is an MSBuild error from Optionary’s targets. The generator runs in every project that references `Optionary`, including through a transitive reference, so these can fire in a consumer of a library too. Except for `OPT0001`, they are reported against source, so `#pragma warning disable` works for the warnings.

| Id                    | Severity | Summary                                                  |
| --------------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`OPT0001`](#opt0001) | Warning  | C# older than 12: nothing is bound                       |
| [`OPT0002`](#opt0002) | Error    | Invalid options type                                     |
| [`OPT0003`](#opt0003) | Error    | Invalid section path                                     |
| [`OPT0004`](#opt0004) | Warning  | Unsupported member                                       |
| [`OPT0005`](#opt0005) | Warning  | Key collision                                            |
| [`OPT0006`](#opt0006) | Error    | Options type can’t be created                            |
| [`OPT0007`](#opt0007) | Warning  | Type graph too large                                     |
| [`OPT0008`](#opt0008) | Warning  | Annotation not expressible in JSON Schema                |
| [`OPT0009`](#opt0009) | Warning  | Schema generation failed                                 |
| [`OPT0010`](#opt0010) | Error    | Options type declared more than once                     |
| [`OPT0011`](#opt0011) | Error    | Key style conflict                                       |
| [`OPT0012`](#opt0012) | Warning  | ZeroAlloc options validation skipped                     |
| [`OPT1001`](#opt1001) | Error    | The runtime is referenced but the generator isn’t loaded |

## OPT0001

[Section titled “OPT0001”](#opt0001)

**The project’s C# version is older than 12.** Warning, reported once per compilation by every project that references `Optionary` (with or without declarations) whose `LangVersion` is below 12:

> Optionary’s source generator needs C# 12 or later, but this project uses C# *version*, so AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions registers nothing and no configuration schema is generated; set LangVersion to 12 or later to enable it

The [registration method](../../guides/registering-from-a-library/) is still emitted, so calls to it compile, but its body is empty: no options type is registered and no fragment is written. Set `LangVersion` to 12 or later. It has no source location, so suppress it with `<NoWarn>` rather than `#pragma`.

## OPT0002

[Section titled “OPT0002”](#opt0002)

**The type can’t be described as configuration:** an interface, a static or abstract class, a struct or enum, an open generic type, or a collection. Declare a class or record class instead.

## OPT0003

[Section titled “OPT0003”](#opt0003)

**The section path isn’t valid for the type:** it is empty, has an empty segment (`A::B`), or was derived from a type name that is only a suffix, such as a class called `Options`. Give the declaration a path: `[Optionary("Section")]`.

## OPT0004

[Section titled “OPT0004”](#opt0004)

**A member has a type configuration binding doesn’t support.** It is left out of the schema and the binder. A `required` member that can’t be bound is set to `default!` so the generated code compiles. See [supported types](../../guides/binding/#supported-types).

## OPT0005

[Section titled “OPT0005”](#opt0005)

**Two members bind the same key.** Keys ignore case, so `Name` and `NAME` collide, as do two members given the same `[ConfigurationKeyName]`. Only the first is described.

## OPT0006

[Section titled “OPT0006”](#opt0006)

**The type can’t be created from configuration:** it has no public constructor, several public constructors with parameters and none without, or a constructor parameter that matches no property.

## OPT0007

[Section titled “OPT0007”](#opt0007)

**The type graph uses too many distinct types** (more than 200), so the schema stops describing them at the member named. Self-expanding generic types report this too.

## OPT0008

[Section titled “OPT0008”](#opt0008)

**An annotation has no JSON Schema equivalent** (a regular expression that can’t be anchored, for example) and is left out of the schema. The member is still bound.

## OPT0009

[Section titled “OPT0009”](#opt0009)

**Schema generation failed unexpectedly for a type.** The type has no schema. Please [report it](https://github.com/RocketSurgeonsGuild/Optionary/issues).

## OPT0010

[Section titled “OPT0010”](#opt0010)

**A type is declared more than once:** by both `[Optionary]` on the class and `[assembly: Optionary<T>]`, or by two assembly attributes. It is reported on the assembly attribute, which contributes nothing. Keep one declaration.

## OPT0011

[Section titled “OPT0011”](#opt0011)

**A type is bound with more than one key style**, because sections with different key styles reach it. The later declaration is reported and contributes nothing. Use the same `KeyStyle` for every section that reaches the type, or give the shared type `[ConfigurationKeyName]` attributes. See [key styles](../../guides/key-styles/#one-spelling-per-type).

## OPT0012

[Section titled “OPT0012”](#opt0012)

**A `[Validate]` type has an asynchronous ZeroAlloc.Validation rule**, so it isn’t validated with `ValidateWithZeroAlloc()`: options validation is synchronous. Make the rule synchronous, or validate the type another way.

## OPT1001

[Section titled “OPT1001”](#opt1001)

**`Optionary` is referenced but its generator isn’t loaded.** Reported by the `_OptionaryCheckGenerator` target in `Optionary.targets`, before `CoreCompile`, when `Optionary.dll` is among the resolved references (`@(ReferencePath)`) and no `@(Analyzer)` item has the file name `Optionary.Analyzers`:

> *Project* references Optionary.dll, but Optionary’s source generator (Optionary.Analyzers) isn’t loaded: no @(Analyzer) item is Optionary.Analyzers, so its \[Optionary] types get no AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions registration method or configuration schema. Look for a target (in the project, a Directory.Build.targets, or another package) that removes Optionary.Analyzers from @(Analyzer), and build with the .NET 10 SDK or later: the package has generators only for Roslyn 5.0 and later, so an older compiler loads none.

Without the generator nothing is bound and no registration method exists.

It happens when:

* a target removes `Optionary.Analyzers` from `@(Analyzer)`; or
* the compiler is older than Roslyn 5.0, so none of the package’s generator slices matches it.

`ExcludeAssets="analyzers"` doesn’t cause it: the .NET SDK passes a package’s analyzers to the compiler whatever the reference excludes, so the generator still runs. `ExcludeAssets="build"` or `"all"` skips `Optionary.targets`, and with it this check; see [troubleshooting](../../troubleshooting/#cs0234-cs0103-or-cs1061-at-a-call-to-addoptionaryconfigurationoptions) for what you see then.

Remove the target, or build with the .NET 10 SDK or later. See [troubleshooting](../../troubleshooting/).

# MSBuild properties

> Every MSBuild property and item metadata Optionary reads, with defaults.

These properties are Optionary’s public MSBuild API. They change only in a major version. Set them in the project file or in a `Directory.Build.props`:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <!-- Permissive: unknown keys under Optionary sections aren't flagged -->
  <OptionarySchemaStrict>false</OptionarySchemaStrict>
</PropertyGroup>
```

## Schema files

[Section titled “Schema files”](#schema-files)

| Property                            | Default  | Effect                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OptionarySchema`                   | on       | `false` writes no schema files, no Visual Studio segments and no editor settings, and removes the files an earlier build wrote.                                                     |
| `OptionarySchemaHost`               | detected | `true` or `false` overrides which projects are hosts. Left empty, test projects (`IsTestProject`) and applications (`OutputType` `Exe` or `WinExe`, or an Android application) are. |
| `OptionarySchemaStrict`             | `true`   | `false` leaves Optionary’s sections open (no `propertyNames` check) in the application schema.                                                                                      |
| `OptionarySchemaIncludeSchemaStore` | `true`   | `false` leaves SchemaStore’s `appsettings.json` schema out of the application schema.                                                                                               |
| `OptionarySchemaCopyToOutput`       | `true`   | `false` keeps a host’s application schema in `obj/`: it isn’t copied to the output directory or published. For hosts that embed their configuration (MAUI, Uno).                    |
| `OptionarySchemaRequired`           | `false`  | `true` lists required members in each fragment’s `required`. The generator reads this one, so it changes the fragments in every project that sets it.                               |
| `OptionaryReferenceDocumentation`   | on       | `false` doesn’t pass referenced packages’ XML documentation files to the generator, so types declared with `[assembly: Optionary<T>]` get no descriptions from them.                |

## Editors

[Section titled “Editors”](#editors)

| Property                           | Default  | Effect                                                                                                                                                                |
| ---------------------------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OptionarySchemaVisualStudio`      | on       | `false` adds no `JsonSchemaSegment` items for Visual Studio; the schema files are still written.                                                                      |
| `OptionaryScaffoldEditorSettings`  | off      | `true` writes Optionary’s mappings into `.vscode/settings.json` when a host builds. See [VS Code](../../guides/schema-and-editors/#let-optionary-write-the-settings). |
| `OptionaryEditorSettingsDirectory` | git root | The folder that holds `.vscode`. Relative paths are relative to the project. By default, the nearest ancestor with a `.git` entry, or the project folder.             |

## Generator

[Section titled “Generator”](#generator)

| Property                       | Default | Effect                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------ | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `RootNamespace`                | SDK     | The namespace of the generated [registration method](../../guides/registering-from-a-library/), used verbatim. Empty or whitespace puts it in the global namespace. |
| `OptionaryZeroAllocValidation` | on      | `false` leaves ZeroAlloc.Validation’s registrations to the project: the registration method doesn’t call `ValidateWithZeroAlloc()`.                                 |
| `LangVersion`                  | SDK     | C# 12 or later is required. Below that the registration method is empty and [`OPT0001`](../diagnostics/#opt0001) is reported.                                       |

## Item metadata

[Section titled “Item metadata”](#item-metadata)

| Item              | Metadata                                 | Effect                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `AdditionalFiles` | `OptionaryReferenceDocumentation="true"` | Marks an XML documentation file the generator reads descriptions from, for types declared with `[assembly: Optionary<T>]`. Optionary adds these itself for package references; add your own for other files. |

## Files

[Section titled “Files”](#files)

| File                                                   | Written by         | What it is                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `$(BaseIntermediateOutputPath)appsettings.schema.json` | hosts              | The application schema, at a stable path (normally `obj/appsettings.schema.json`). Copied to `$(OutDir)` and published unless `OptionarySchemaCopyToOutput` is `false`. |
| `$(IntermediateOutputPath)appsettings.schema.json`     | multi-target hosts | The application schema for each target framework after the first.                                                                                                       |
| `$(IntermediateOutputPath)ConfigurationSchema.json`    | libraries          | The library schema, packed at the package root.                                                                                                                         |

## For host frameworks

[Section titled “For host frameworks”](#for-host-frameworks)

A framework that builds on Optionary can set `OptionarySchemaHost`, `OptionarySchemaCopyToOutput` and `OptionaryZeroAllocValidation` from its own targets. Optionary reads them when the schema is computed, not at evaluation, so a value set anywhere during evaluation counts, and setting them has no effect in a project that doesn’t reference Optionary. Dovetail does this from its application detection and its embedded-configuration and ZeroAlloc switches.

# Troubleshooting

> What to check when the generator doesn't run, the registration method is missing, or the schema isn't there.

## The generator isn’t loaded

[Section titled “The generator isn’t loaded”](#the-generator-isnt-loaded)

The build fails with [`OPT1001`](../reference/diagnostics/#opt1001): `Optionary` is referenced, but its generator isn’t among the compiler’s analyzers (`@(Analyzer)`). Nothing is bound and the registration method doesn’t exist.

* **A target removes the generator.** Look for a target, in the project, a `Directory.Build.targets` or another package, that removes `Optionary.Analyzers` from `@(Analyzer)`, and remove it.
* **The compiler is too old.** The package carries the generator for Roslyn 5.0 and later, so an older compiler matches no slice and loads none. Build with the .NET 10 SDK or later, and check that `global.json` doesn’t pin an older one.

`ExcludeAssets="analyzers"` on the package reference doesn’t cause this: the .NET SDK passes a package’s analyzers to the compiler whatever the reference excludes, so the generator still runs.

## CS0234, CS0103 or CS1061 at a call to `AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions`

[Section titled “CS0234, CS0103 or CS1061 at a call to AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions”](#cs0234-cs0103-or-cs1061-at-a-call-to-addoptionaryconfigurationoptions)

If Optionary’s build assets are excluded (`ExcludeAssets="build"` or `ExcludeAssets="all"`, or an `IncludeAssets` without `build`), its `.props` and `.targets` aren’t imported, so the `OPT1001` check doesn’t run either. The generator still runs, but `RootNamespace` isn’t passed to it (Optionary’s `CompilerVisibleProperty`), so it puts `OptionaryConfigurationOptions` in the global namespace. The schema targets don’t run, so there’s no `appsettings.schema.json` either.

A `using <RootNamespace>;` then doesn’t find the method (CS1061: `IServiceCollection` has no `AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions`), and a fully qualified call to `<RootNamespace>.OptionaryConfigurationOptions` fails with CS0234 (or CS0103). In a Dovetail application the error is in Dovetail’s generated exports file, at the joint that calls `global::<RootNamespace>.OptionaryConfigurationOptions.AddOptionaryConfigurationOptions`: CS0234.

Include the package’s `build` assets.

## The registration method isn’t found, but the generator runs

[Section titled “The registration method isn’t found, but the generator runs”](#the-registration-method-isnt-found-but-the-generator-runs)

* **Missing `using`.** The method is in the project’s `RootNamespace`. Top-level statements are in the global namespace, so `Program.cs` needs `using <RootNamespace>;`.
* **Old C#.** Below C# 12 the method exists but is empty, with [`OPT0001`](../reference/diagnostics/#opt0001).
* **CS0436.** Two assemblies with the same `RootNamespace`, one with `InternalsVisibleTo` the other, both define `OptionaryConfigurationOptions`. Give them distinct `RootNamespace`s.

## An options type isn’t bound

[Section titled “An options type isn’t bound”](#an-options-type-isnt-bound)

* Check the build for `OPT` errors: a rejected declaration contributes nothing.
* `RegisterOptions = false` only describes the section; bind the type yourself.
* Named options aren’t registered: `IOptionsMonitor<T>.Get("name")` throws for any name but the default.
* Under the `Dash` or `Underscore` [key style](../guides/key-styles/), `MaxFileSizeMb` in the configuration doesn’t bind; write `max-file-size-mb` or `max_file_size_mb`.

## No schema, or a section is missing from it

[Section titled “No schema, or a section is missing from it”](#no-schema-or-a-section-is-missing-from-it)

* Build the project: the file is written after compilation.
* Only hosts write `appsettings.schema.json`. A library writes `ConfigurationSchema.json` instead. Set `OptionarySchemaHost` to `true` if a project should be a host.
* `OptionarySchema` set to `false` turns all schema files off.
* The application schema only covers assemblies the host references, and only declarations that weren’t rejected.
* Libraries packed with Dovetail 0.4 or 0.5 carry `Dovetail.ConfigurationSchema.v1:` fragments, which Optionary doesn’t read. Rebuild them with Optionary.

[Schema and editors](../guides/schema-and-editors/#when-completion-doesnt-work) covers editor-side problems.
